answer.answer:
Adopting a robotic process is mostly a change to how the work is organised and contracted, not a change of kit: of the things that have to be in place, the robotic arm is the only machine, and the rest are a delivery model, business model and work culture that fit robotics, workforce training, early contractor involvement, vertical integration, a coordinating design role, prefabrication and a highly standardised product. These requirements are not equal in weight: workforce training is drawn on by 44 of the 50 coded cases and standardisation and vertical integration by 25 each, while the coordinating role appears in 8 and regulatory concern in 12. The delivery-model change itself is asserted for robotic assembly by only 2 of the 50 cases, and is carried far more strongly as a condition of industrialised production, drawn on by 13, so treat it as the price of scaling rather than of a single robotic task. Nothing in the material links the deployed Japanese records to particular enablers, so the specific delivery changes those firms made are not in front of you.

**The delivery model itself**

The direct statement is that robotic assembly (PR4) depends on Delivery/business model/work culture (RI12), on the grounds that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [1], backed by peer-reviewed evidence. Read the direction carefully: RI12 is the requirement and comes first in practice. That edge is carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases [2], while RI12 is drawn on by 16 of the 50 [2]. The same requirement appears more strongly one level up: AT8 "Industrialised" also depends on RI12, on the grounds that adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models, and that edge is carried by 13 of the 50 cases [2]. RI12 is a Risk, an exposure rather than an activity, and it carries 2 inbound and 0 outbound dependency edges [2]: everything asserted about it positions it as something to be addressed, with nothing asserted as following from it.

**Contracting and organisational form**

Early contractor involvement (CO11) enables an integrated design-DFAB process (AT12), on the grounds that BIM and early contractor involvement improve design management and increase DFAB adoption [2]; it also enables prefabrication/off-site (PR2), because integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party to be involved in the early design phase and a delivery method that involves participants in early design should be selected [2]; and it enables DfMA for the DFAB process (PR9), early collaboration being among the DfMA enablers [2]. These three are carried by 10, 13 and 11 of the 50 cases respectively, against 14 of the 50 drawing on early contractor involvement itself [2].

Organisational form runs alongside it in both directions: an integrated design-DFAB process has vertical integration (CO10) as a precondition, on the mirroring argument that technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm [2], and vertical integration is also named as enabling that integrated process among management approaches for digital fabrication adoption, though that second citation is self-declared correlational [2]; both edges are carried by 14 of the 50. The lighter-weight option is a role rather than a restructuring: a DFAB design coordinator (AC4) enables the integrated design-DFAB process through interdisciplinary team integration, carried by 7 of the 50 [2], and 8 of the 50 cases draw on that role [2] against 25 for vertical integration [2]. Scheduling discipline is a further delivery change: Lean (PR18) has task schedule planning (AR14) as a precondition, because production with short takt requires a highly detailed definition of tasks to avoid ambiguousness [2], carried by 13 of the 50, with 28 of the 50 drawing on task schedule planning [2].

**Workforce, safety and compliance**

Human-robot interaction (CO6) depends on addressing the requirement for workforce training (RI6), because the success of human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce [2]; that edge is carried by 27 of the 50, the heaviest in this set, and 44 of the 50 cases draw on workforce training [2]. Human-robot interaction also depends on regulatory/legal concern (RI18) through compliance with robot safety standards [2], on standards evidence, carried by only 2 of the 50; and in the other direction it mitigates work safety concern (RI20), power-and-force-limiting collaborative operation within biomechanical limits mitigating contact-injury risk [2], also on standards evidence, carried by 4. The context names specific robot safety standards but gives no count of the regulatory instruments in the record, so treat the compliance picture here as partial rather than complete.

**What the process needs technically, and what it returns**

Robotic assembly depends on a robotic arm (RE2) [2], carried by 12 of the 50, the mirror of the arm enabling that assembly [2]. It also has prefabrication/off-site as a precondition, automated overhead delivery and assembly requiring extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [2], carried by 4; "Highly standardised" (AT7) enables it, Japanese automated erection systems relying on standardised prefabricated components [2], carried by 10; and path-planning (PR12) enables it as a precondition [2], carried by 2. One asserted enabler is exhibited by nobody: "Mobile factory" (CO12), a Condition, is cited as enabling robotic assembly through all-weather cover allowing welding and assembly to proceed in rain, and that edge is carried by 0 of the 50 coded cases [2], cited in the literature and carried by none of the 50, with 1 of the 50 cases drawing on the condition at all [2]. On the return side, robotic assembly amplifies reduced time and improved productivity (VA2), carried by 13 of the 50 [2], amplifies reduced cost (VA6), carried by 7 [2], and enables reduced errors and constraints (VA10) through quality control, carried by 1 [2].

**The deployed record**

Two of the deployed processes here perform assembly. census_RXH4-1 was adopted to address cost and labor, performs assembly and concrete work on the structural core and the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, and sits at technology readiness level 9 [3], with Firm_166 as its manufacturer and concrete as its material [4]. census_RXH7-2 was adopted to address quality, safety, labor and market, performs assembly and tiling on the building envelope, facade or curtain wall, and is also at technology readiness level 9 [5]; it is a census record of process RP29, with Firm_125 as manufacturer, working in ceramic and steel [4]. These records tell you what pressures drove adoption, but the context does not link either case, or the sitework, cleaning, envelope and timber-joinery records alongside them, to any enabler, so they cannot be used to say which of the delivery changes above were actually made. Retrieval also read "adopt" as including reliance on a DFAB specialist and risk-sharing or agile contracting; the context carries neither counts nor edges for those, so nothing can be said here about contractual risk-sharing either way.
